assessment.nobel_worthiness: A major empirical and conceptual advance that made intergenerational mobility measurable at population scale and changed the study of inequality and opportunity.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren and Friedman are central to the administrative-data research program represented by this contribution.
assessment.maturity: The approach has generated a substantial, influential body of evidence and a durable research agenda.
uncertainties: The contribution includes a wider collaborative research network, making the three-person attribution necessarily selective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work provided compelling evidence and a coherent framework for understanding how technology and trade reshape local labour markets, employment and inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the clearest core contributors to the linked evidence on tasks, trade exposure and labour-demand change.
assessment.maturity: Its empirical findings and methods have been extensively debated, extended and incorporated into labour and trade research.
uncertainties: Separating the contribution of trade shocks from broader technological and regional forces remains empirically demanding.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence studies made discrimination directly measurable in consequential market settings and reshaped empirical work on unequal treatment.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are especially central to the canonical correspondence-study contribution; Charles represents the broader labour-discrimination program.
assessment.maturity: The design has been replicated across settings and has had sustained influence on research and public debate.
uncertainties: The candidate grouping combines several related designs and literatures whose intellectual origins extend beyond these three researchers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The evidence that early-life conditions have lasting effects on health, education and economic outcomes has transformed policy-relevant human-capital research.
assessment.attribution: Currie, Almond and Cunha make complementary central contributions through empirical identification and dynamic skill-formation frameworks.
assessment.maturity: The literature is broad, long-running and influential across health, education and labour economics.
uncertainties: The contribution spans distinct mechanisms and methods, so a single tightly bounded prize citation would require careful formulation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The modern analysis of monopsony restored employer market power to the center of labour economics and altered the interpretation of wages and policy.
assessment.attribution: Manning supplied a defining theoretical synthesis, while Naidu and Ashenfelter represent important empirical and institutional advances.
assessment.maturity: The framework has become central to contemporary labour-market analysis and supports a substantial empirical literature.
uncertainties: The listed contribution covers a large body of theory and evidence with potentially broader claims to credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The demonstration and modeling of reciprocity, fairness and inequity aversion substantially expanded economic accounts of behaviour and institutions.
assessment.attribution: Fehr and Schmidt are especially closely associated with formalizing inequity aversion; Falk is a leading contributor to the experimental evidence and broader program.
assessment.maturity: The concepts are long established, widely tested and influential across experimental, labour and organizational economics.
uncertainties: The evidence on how stable and context-independent social preferences are remains contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The integration of insurance theory with credible empirical measurement advanced understanding of adverse selection and the design of insurance markets.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein, Einav and Salanie are prominent and complementary contributors to the theory-measurement connection in this area.
assessment.maturity: The work has accumulated across health, credit and other insurance contexts and is firmly embedded in applied microeconomics.
uncertainties: Adverse selection and moral hazard are often jointly present, complicating clean empirical separation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collective models replaced unitary accounts of households with an empirically meaningful analysis of bargaining, distribution and individual incentives within families.
assessment.attribution: Chiappori supplied foundational identification and collective-model theory, while Lundberg and Pollak made major contributions to household bargaining and empirical application.
assessment.maturity: The approach has had durable influence in family, labour and development economics.
uncertainties: Empirical identification of bargaining power and intra-household allocations remains sensitive to modeling assumptions.
